Additive bases and the zero-sum invariant 𝖭⁡(G)\mathsf{N}(G) for groups Cp⊕Cn​pC_{p}\oplus C_{np}Thanks: This work was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 12071344).

Wenkai Yang Address: Center for Combinatorics, Nankai University, Tianjin 300071, P.R. China Email address: 3016210052@tju.edu.cn; 9820250116@nankai.edu.cn
Abstract.

Let GG be a finite abelian group, and let c0​(G)c_{0}(G) be the least integer such that every regular sequence over GG of at least this length is an additive basis. Let 𝖭⁡(G)\mathsf{N}(G) be the least integer ll such that every weak-regular sequence SS over GG with |S|≥l|S|\geq l has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence TT satisfying 𝗏g​(T)=𝗏g​(S)\mathsf{v}_{g}(T)=\mathsf{v}_{g}(S) for some g|Sg\mid S. We obtain a common upper bound for c0​(Cq⊕Cn​q)c_{0}(C_{q}\oplus C_{nq}) for groups of odd order, where qq is prime, and prove 𝖭⁡(G)≥r⁡(nr−1)+1\mathsf{N}(G)\geq r(n_{r}-1)+1 when G=Cn1⊕⋯⊕CnrG=C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}} with 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r}. If n≥1n\geq 1 and p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime divisor of n​pnp, we obtain 𝖭⁡(Cp⊕Cn​p2)=2​n​p2−1\mathsf{N}(C_{p}\oplus C_{np^{2}})=2np^{2}-1 and give upper bounds for 𝖭⁡(Cp⊕Cn​p)\mathsf{N}(C_{p}\oplus C_{np}) when p∤np\nmid n. We also determine 𝖭⁡(Cn)\mathsf{N}(C_{n}) for two infinite families of cyclic groups arising in earlier work.

Key words and phrases: 
finite abelian group, additive basis, regular sequence, zero-sum subsequence
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11B75; Secondary 11A07, 20K01

1. Introduction and main results

Let GG be a finite abelian group, with additive notation, and let SS be a sequence over GG. Denote by ∑(S)\sum(S) the set of sums of nonempty subsequences of SS. The sequence SS is an additive basis of GG if ∑(S)=G\sum(S)=G. For a subgroup H≤GH\leq G, let SHS_{H} be the subsequence consisting of all terms of SS in HH. We call SS regular over GG if |SH|≤|H|−1|S_{H}|\leq|H|-1 for every proper subgroup H<GH<G. Let c0​(G)c_{0}(G) be the least integer ll such that every regular sequence over GG of length at least ll is an additive basis. The problem of determining c0​(G)c_{0}(G) was proposed by Olson; see [2, 6].

Let pp be the smallest prime divisor of |G||G|, and let

m⁡(G)={|G|,G​ is cyclic,2​p−1,G=Cp2,n​p+2​p−3,G=Cp⊕Cn​p,n≥2,|G|/p+p−2,otherwise.m(G)=\begin{cases}|G|,&G\text{ is cyclic},\\ 2p-1,&G=C_{p}^{2},\\ np+2p-3,&G=C_{p}\oplus C_{np},\ n\geq 2,\\ |G|/p+p-2,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The inequality c0​(G)≥m⁡(G)c_{0}(G)\geq m(G) is known for every finite abelian group [6, Lemma 2.3]. Equality has been established for many groups of rank at least three; see [2, 6]. For a group G=Cn1⊕Cn2G=C_{n_{1}}\oplus C_{n_{2}} with 1<n1|n21<n_{1}\mid n_{2}, the known cases include the following:

  1. (1)

    |G||G| is even, or GG is a pp-group [2, 10];

  2. (2)

    G=C3⊕C3​qG=C_{3}\oplus C_{3q}, where q≥5q\geq 5 is prime [11];

  3. (3)

    p≥3p\geq 3, n1≥2​pn_{1}\geq 2p and |G|≥72​p6|G|\geq 72p^{6} [5];

  4. (4)

    p≥11p\geq 11 and n1≥p2n_{1}\geq p^{2} [12].

Qu, Li, Wang and Zhao also proved that c0​(G)≤2​|G|/5+1c_{0}(G)\leq 2|G|/5+1 for every group of rank two with p≥11p\geq 11 [12, Lemma 7]. For G=Cp⊕Cn​pG=C_{p}\oplus C_{np} with n≥2n\geq 2, Qu and Han conjectured that c0​(G)=n​p+2​p−3c_{0}(G)=np+2p-3 [10, Concluding Remark].

We also study the invariant 𝖭⁡(G)\mathsf{N}(G) introduced by Gao et al. [3]. A sequence SS over GG is weak-regular if 𝗏g​(S)≤ord⁡(g)\mathsf{v}_{g}(S)\leq\ord(g) for every g∈Gg\in G, where 𝗏g​(S)\mathsf{v}_{g}(S) denotes the multiplicity of gg in SS. The invariant 𝖭⁡(G)\mathsf{N}(G) is the least integer ll such that every weak-regular sequence SS over GG with |S|≥l|S|\geq l has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence TT satisfying 𝗏g​(T)=𝗏g​(S)\mathsf{v}_{g}(T)=\mathsf{v}_{g}(S) for some g|Sg\mid S. Equivalently, supp⁡(S​T−1)≠supp⁡(S)\supp(ST^{-1})\neq\supp(S). Gao et al. determined 𝖭⁡(Cpr)=r⁡(p−1)+1\mathsf{N}(C_{p}^{r})=r(p-1)+1 for p≤3p\leq 3 and 𝖭⁡(Cp2)=4​p−2​⌈2​p+1⌉+1\mathsf{N}(C_{p}^{2})=4p-2\lceil 2\sqrt{p+1}\rceil+1 for p≥3p\geq 3 [4, Theorem 1.3]. For cyclic groups, Jiang and the author proved

2​n−⌈2​n+1⌉≤𝖭⁡(Cn)≤2​n−⌈2​n+1⌉+1(n≥3),2n-\lceil 2\sqrt{n+1}\rceil\leq\mathsf{N}(C_{n})\leq 2n-\lceil 2\sqrt{n+1}\rceil+1\qquad(n\geq 3),

with each equality holding for infinitely many nn [8, Theorem 1.1].

Our bounds for additive bases follow from the estimate

c0​(Cq⊕Cn​q)≤max⁡{n​q+2​q2−q−1,n​q​(q+1)p−q+p−2},c_{0}(C_{q}\oplus C_{nq})\leq\max\left\{nq+2q^{2}-q-1,\,\frac{nq(q+1)}{p}-q+p-2\right\},

where qq is prime, n≥2n\geq 2, and p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime divisor of n​qnq; see Theorem 3.5. This estimate applies whether or not q|nq\mid n. The first two theorems give consequences for the two cases separately.

Theorem 1.1.

Let qq be prime and let G=Cq⊕Cn​q2G=C_{q}\oplus C_{nq^{2}}, where n≥1n\geq 1 is not a power of qq. If p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime dividing |G||G|, then

c0​(G)≤max⁡{n​q2​(q+1)p,n​q2+f⁡(q)−1},\displaystyle c_{0}(G)\leq\max\{\frac{nq^{2}(q+1)}{p},nq^{2}+f(q)-1\},

where f⁡(q)=4​q​(q−1)+1f(q)=4q(q-1)+1 for q≥7q\geq 7, f⁡(q)=2​q2+3f(q)=2q^{2}+3 for q≤5q\leq 5.

Theorem 1.2.

Let qq be prime and let G=Cq⊕Cn​qG=C_{q}\oplus C_{nq}, where n≥1n\geq 1 and q∤nq\nmid n. If p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime dividing |G||G|, then

c0​(G)≤max⁡{(2​q−1)​(n+q+1),n​q2p+2​n​qp}.\displaystyle c_{0}(G)\leq\max\{(2q-1)(n+q+1),\frac{nq^{2}}{p}+2\frac{nq}{p}\}.

For 𝖭⁡(G)\mathsf{N}(G), we prove the lower bound r⁡(nr−1)+1r(n_{r}-1)+1. The other term in the following theorem is the direct-sum bound of Gao et al. [4, Theorem 1.1(2)].

Theorem 1.3.

Let G=Cn1⊕⋯⊕CnrG=C_{n_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_{r}}, where 1<n1​∣⋯∣​nr1<n_{1}\mid\cdots\mid n_{r}. Then

𝖭⁡(G)≥max⁡{r⁡(nr−1)+1,∑i=1r(𝖭⁡(Cni)−1)+1}.\mathsf{N}(G)\geq\max\left\{r(n_{r}-1)+1,\ \sum_{i=1}^{r}\bigl(\mathsf{N}(C_{n_{i}})-1\bigr)+1\right\}.
Theorem 1.4.

Let G=Cp⊕Cn​pG=C_{p}\oplus C_{np}, where n≥2n\geq 2 and p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime dividing |G||G|. Then

2​n​p−1≤𝖭⁡(G)≤{2​n​p−1,p|n,5​n​p−4,p≥5,p∤n,4​n​p−3,p=3, 3∤n.2np-1\leq\mathsf{N}(G)\leq\begin{cases}2np-1,&p\mid n,\\ 5np-4,&p\geq 5,\ p\nmid n,\\ 4np-3,&p=3,\ 3\nmid n.\end{cases}

In particular, 𝖭⁡(Cp⊕Cn​p2)=2​n​p2−1\mathsf{N}(C_{p}\oplus C_{np^{2}})=2np^{2}-1 whenever n≥1n\geq 1 and p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime dividing the group order. The two upper bounds for p∤np\nmid n also hold when n=1n=1.

Section 2 gives the notation and preliminary lemmas. Section 3 proves Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. Section 4 proves Theorems 1.3 and 1.4. The final section discusses the remaining rank-two cases and two cyclic families.

2. Notation and preliminaries

Our notation for sequences follows the standard conventions of zero-sum theory; see [1, 7]. A sequence over GG is finite and unordered, and repetitions are allowed. For a sequence S=g1⋯glS=g_{1}\cdots g_{l}, its length is |S|=l|S|=l, its sum is σ⁡(S)=g1+⋯+gl\sigma(S)=g_{1}+\cdots+g_{l}, and its support is supp⁡(S)={g∈G:𝗏g​(S)>0}\supp(S)=\{g\in G:\mathsf{v}_{g}(S)>0\}. The relation T|ST\mid S means that TT is a subsequence of SS; then S​T−1ST^{-1} is the subsequence obtained by deleting TT from SS. The empty sequence is denoted by 11 and has sum 00. Two subsequences T1,T2T_{1},T_{2} of SS are disjoint if T1​T2|ST_{1}T_{2}\mid S. A homomorphism φ:G→G1\varphi:G\to G_{1} induces the sequence φ(S)=φ(g1)⋯φ(gl)\varphi(S)=\varphi(g_{1})\cdots\varphi(g_{l}) over G1G_{1}.

Let ∑0(S)={0}∪∑(S)\sum_{0}(S)=\{0\}\cup\sum(S). Thus ∑0(S)\sum_{0}(S) includes the sum of the empty subsequence, whereas ∑(S)\sum(S) consists of sums of nonempty subsequences. A nonempty sequence is a minimal zero-sum sequence if it has sum 00 and no proper nonempty zero-sum subsequence. The Davenport constant 𝖣⁡(G)\mathsf{D}(G) is the least integer ll such that every sequence over GG of length at least ll has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence. We use 𝖣⁡(Cn1⊕Cn2)=n1+n2−1\mathsf{D}(C_{n_{1}}\oplus C_{n_{2}})=n_{1}+n_{2}-1 for 1≤n1|n21\leq n_{1}\mid n_{2} [7, Theorem 5.8.3]. Let ℕ\mathbb{N} denote the positive integers. We use the usual floor and ceiling functions ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor and ⌈x⌉\lceil x\rceil.

For each subset AA of GG, denote by st⁡(A)={g∈G:g+A=A}\st(A)=\{g\in G:g+A=A\} the stabilizer of AA in GG. Then st⁡(A)\st(A) is the maximal subgroup HH of GG such that H+A=AH+A=A. We use the following form of Kneser’s theorem; see [9, Theorem 4.4].

Lemma 2.1 (Kneser).

Let A1,…,AnA_{1},...,A_{n} be nonempty finite subsets of an abelian group GG, and H=st⁡(A1+⋯+An)H=\st(A_{1}+\cdots+A_{n}) be the stabilizer. Then

|A1+⋯+An|≥|A1+H|+⋯+|An+H|−(n−1)​|H|.|A_{1}+\cdots+A_{n}|\geq|A_{1}+H|+\cdots+|A_{n}+H|-(n-1)|H|.
Lemma 2.2 (Cauchy–Davenport).

Let A1,…,AnA_{1},...,A_{n} be nonempty finite subsets of an abelian group G=CpG=C_{p}, where pp is prime. Then

|A1+⋯+An|≥min⁡{p,|A1|+⋯+|An|−(n−1)}.|A_{1}+\cdots+A_{n}|\geq\min\{p,\,|A_{1}|+\cdots+|A_{n}|-(n-1)\}.
Lemma 2.3.

For every finite abelian group GG,

m⁡(G)≤c0​(G)≤|G|.m(G)\leq c_{0}(G)\leq|G|.

See [6, Lemma 2.3] for the lower bound and [2, Lemma 2.4] for the upper bound.

Qu and Han determined c0​(G)c_{0}(G) for G=Cp⊕CpnG=C_{p}\oplus C_{p^{n}} as follows.

Lemma 2.4 ([10]).

Let G=Cp⊕CpnG=C_{p}\oplus C_{p^{n}}, where pp is prime and n≥2n\geq 2. Then

c0​(G)=pn+2​p−3.c_{0}(G)=p^{n}+2p-3.
Lemma 2.5 ([2, Lemma 2.3(1)]).

Let GG be a finite abelian group, and let pp be the smallest prime dividing |G||G|. Let SS be a regular sequence over GG of length |S|≥max⁡{|G|/p+p−2,𝖣⁡(G)}|S|\geq\max\{|G|/p+p-2,~\mathsf{D}(G)\}. If ∑(S)≠G\sum(S)\neq G, then st⁡(∑(S))={0}\st(\sum(S))=\{0\}.

We use the cyclic bound

𝖭⁡(Cn)≤2​n−⌈2​n+1⌉+1(n≥3)\mathsf{N}(C_{n})\leq 2n-\lceil 2\sqrt{n+1}\rceil+1\qquad(n\geq 3)

from [8, Theorem 1.1], and the value 𝖭⁡(Cp2)=4​p−2​⌈2​p+1⌉+1\mathsf{N}(C_{p}^{2})=4p-2\lceil 2\sqrt{p+1}\rceil+1 for p≥3p\geq 3 from [4, Theorem 1.3(3)]. Also 𝖭⁡(C2)=2\mathsf{N}(C_{2})=2.

Lemma 2.6.

Let G=Cp⊕Cn​pG=C_{p}\oplus C_{np}, where p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime divisor of |G||G|. For 1<m|n1<m\mid n, let H≤p​GH\leq pG have order mm, and let k=n/mk=n/m. Then

2​n​p−1−(𝖭⁡(H)−1+(m−1)​k​p)≥{2​k​p−1,p|k,m≠n,4​k​p−3,p=3,p∤k,m≠n,5​k​p−4,p≥5,p∤k,m≠n,𝖭⁡(Cp2),m=n.2np-1-\bigl(\mathsf{N}(H)-1+(m-1)kp\bigr)\geq\begin{cases}2kp-1,&p\mid k,\ m\neq n,\\ 4kp-3,&p=3,\ p\nmid k,\ m\neq n,\\ 5kp-4,&p\geq 5,\ p\nmid k,\ m\neq n,\\ \mathsf{N}(C_{p}^{2}),&m=n.\end{cases}
Proof.

Since m≥p≥3m\geq p\geq 3, the cyclic bound gives 𝖭⁡(H)≤2​m−3\mathsf{N}(H)\leq 2m-3. Therefore

2​n​p−1−(𝖭⁡(H)−1+(m−1)​k​p)\displaystyle 2np-1-\bigl(\mathsf{N}(H)-1+(m-1)kp\bigr) =k​p​(m+1)−𝖭⁡(H)\displaystyle=kp(m+1)-\mathsf{N}(H)
≥k​p​(m+1)−2​m+3.\displaystyle\geq kp(m+1)-2m+3.

For m<nm<n, subtracting 2​k​p−12kp-1 from the last expression gives (k​p−2)​(m−1)+2≥0(kp-2)(m-1)+2\geq 0. When p=3p=3, subtracting 4​k​p−34kp-3 gives (m−3)​(k​p−2)≥0(m-3)(kp-2)\geq 0. When p≥5p\geq 5, subtracting 5​k​p−45kp-4 gives (m−4)​k​p−2​m+7≥3​m−13>0(m-4)kp-2m+7\geq 3m-13>0. These prove the first three estimates. If m=nm=n, then k=1k=1, and the left side is at least

(p−2)​n+p+3≥p2−p+3>4​p−7≥𝖭⁡(Cp2).(p-2)n+p+3\geq p^{2}-p+3>4p-7\geq\mathsf{N}(C_{p}^{2}).

The strict inequality follows from p2−5​p+10=(p−2)​(p−3)+4>0p^{2}-5p+10=(p-2)(p-3)+4>0. ∎

Lemma 2.7.

Let SS be a weak-regular sequence over G=CnG=C_{n}, where n≥2n\geq 2 and |S|≥n|S|\geq n. Then either ∑(S)=G\sum(S)=G, or there is a zero-sum subsequence T|ST\mid S such that 𝗏g​(T)=𝗏g​(S)≥1\mathsf{v}_{g}(T)=\mathsf{v}_{g}(S)\geq 1 for some g|Sg\mid S.

Proof.

If 𝗏g​(S)=ord⁡(g)\mathsf{v}_{g}(S)=\ord(g) for some gg, take T=gord⁡(g)T=g^{\ord(g)}. Otherwise 0∉supp⁡(S)0\notin\supp(S), and we may assume ∑(S)≠G\sum(S)\neq G. Since |S|≥𝖣⁡(G)|S|\geq\mathsf{D}(G), ∑(S)=∑0(S)\sum(S)=\sum_{0}(S). Let H=st⁡(∑0(S))H=\st(\sum_{0}(S)) and m=|H|m=|H|. If m=1m=1, Kneser’s theorem gives |∑0(S)|≥|S|+1>n|\sum_{0}(S)|\geq|S|+1>n. Thus m>1m>1, and ∑0(S)≠G\sum_{0}(S)\neq G gives m<nm<n. Since n=d​mn=dm for some integer d≥2d\geq 2, Kneser’s theorem also gives

(|S|−|SH|+1)​m≤|∑0(S)|≤n−m,|SH|≥n−d+2≥2​m≥𝖭⁡(H).(|S|-|S_{H}|+1)m\leq\bigl|\sum_{0}(S)\bigr|\leq n-m,\qquad|S_{H}|\geq n-d+2\geq 2m\geq\mathsf{N}(H).

The middle inequality is equivalent to (d−2)​(m−1)≥0(d-2)(m-1)\geq 0. Apply the definition of 𝖭⁡(H)\mathsf{N}(H) to the weak-regular sequence SHS_{H}; all occurrences in SS of the resulting element g∈Hg\in H belong to SHS_{H}. ∎

Lemma 2.8.

Let S,S′S,S^{\prime} be sequences over a finite abelian group GG, and let H≤GH\leq G satisfy H⊆∑0(S)H\subseteq\sum_{0}(S). Suppose that T1|S′T_{1}\mid S^{\prime} satisfies σ⁡(T1)∈H\sigma(T_{1})\in H and 𝗏g​(T1)=𝗏g​(S′)≥1\mathsf{v}_{g}(T_{1})=\mathsf{v}_{g}(S^{\prime})\geq 1 for some g∈supp⁡(S′)∖supp⁡(S)g\in\supp(S^{\prime})\setminus\supp(S). 3. Proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2

Lemma 3.1.

Let SS be a regular sequence over a finite abelian group GG. Then

|∑0(S)|≥min⁡{|G|,|S|+1}.|\sum_{0}(S)|\geq\min\{|G|,|S|+1\}.

In particular, ∑0(S)=G\sum_{0}(S)=G if |S|≥|G|−1|S|\geq|G|-1.

Proof.

Suppose that |∑0(S)|<min⁡{|G|,|S|+1}|\sum_{0}(S)|<\min\{|G|,|S|+1\}. Let H=st⁡(∑0(S))H=\st(\sum_{0}(S)) and m=|H|m=|H|. Then H<GH<G and m≤|S|m\leq|S|, so Kneser’s theorem gives

|∑0(S)|≥(|S|−|SH|+1)​m≥(|S|−m+2)​m≥|S|+1,|\sum_{0}(S)|\geq(|S|-|S_{H}|+1)m\geq(|S|-m+2)m\geq|S|+1,

a contradiction. ∎

Let K<H<GK<H<G, where |K|≥2|K|\geq 2 and H/K≅CqH/K\cong C_{q} for a prime qq. Let SS be a sequence over H∖KH\setminus K that is regular over GG. If |S|≥2​q−1|S|\geq 2q-1, then there exists T|ST\mid S such that |T|≤q|T|\leq q and σ⁡(T)∈K∖{0}\sigma(T)\in K\setminus\{0\}.

Proof.

Take R​R′|SRR^{\prime}\mid S with |R|=q|R|=q and |R′|=q−1|R^{\prime}|=q-1. Since RR is regular over HH and |H|=q​|K|≥2​q|H|=q|K|\geq 2q, Lemma 3.1 gives |∑0(R)|≥q+1|\sum_{0}(R)|\geq q+1. Thus there exist R1,R2|RR_{1},R_{2}\mid R whose sums are distinct and belong to the same coset of KK. By Cauchy–Davenport, ∑0(R′)+K=H\sum_{0}(R^{\prime})+K=H. Choose R3|R′R_{3}\mid R^{\prime} such that σ⁡(R1​R3),σ⁡(R2​R3)∈K\sigma(R_{1}R_{3}),\sigma(R_{2}R_{3})\in K. Choose U∈{R1​R3,R2​R3}U\in\{R_{1}R_{3},R_{2}R_{3}\} with σ⁡(U)≠0\sigma(U)\neq 0. Factor UU into subsequences whose images in H/KH/K are minimal zero-sum sequences. Each factor has length at most qq, and at least one has nonzero sum, as required. ∎

Lemma 3.3.

Let K≤GK\leq G with |K|≥2|K|\geq 2 and G/K≅Cq2G/K\cong C_{q}^{2} for a prime qq. If SS is regular over GG and

|S|≥q​|K|+2​q2−q−1,|S|\geq q|K|+2q^{2}-q-1,

then S=SKT1⋯TkRS=S_{K}T_{1}\cdots T_{k}R, where k=|K|−|SK|k=|K|-|S_{K}|, |Ti|≤q|T_{i}|\leq q, σ⁡(Ti)∈K∖{0}\sigma(T_{i})\in K\setminus\{0\} and ∑0(R)+K=G\sum_{0}(R)+K=G.

Proof.

Let φ:G→G/K\varphi:G\to G/K be the natural homomorphism and let k=|K|−|SK|k=|K|-|S_{K}|. Starting with S​SK−1SS_{K}^{-1}, choose at each step a subgroup of order qq containing the largest number of remaining images. Before each of the first kk steps, the remaining length is at least |S|−|SK|−q⁡(k−1)≥2​q2−1|S|-|S_{K}|-q(k-1)\geq 2q^{2}-1, so the chosen subgroup contains at least 2​q−12q-1 terms. Apply Lemma 3.2 in its inverse image to obtain T1,…,TkT_{1},\ldots,T_{k}. The remaining sequence R=S(SKT1⋯Tk)−1R=S(S_{K}T_{1}\cdots T_{k})^{-1} has length |R|≥2​q2−q−1|R|\geq 2q^{2}-q-1. Suppose that ∑0(φ⁡(R))≠G/K\sum_{0}(\varphi(R))\neq G/K. Since |R|>(q+1)​(q−2)|R|>(q+1)(q-2), some subgroup H¯\bar{H} of order qq contains at least q−1q-1 terms of φ⁡(R)\varphi(R). For H=φ−1​(H¯)H=\varphi^{-1}(\bar{H}), Cauchy–Davenport gives ∑0(φ⁡(RH))=H¯\sum_{0}(\varphi(R_{H}))=\bar{H}. It also gives |R​RH−1|≤q−2|RR_{H}^{-1}|\leq q-2, since otherwise ∑0(φ⁡(R))=G/K\sum_{0}(\varphi(R))=G/K. Thus |RH|≥2​q2−2​q+1|R_{H}|\geq 2q^{2}-2q+1. Working backwards, suppose that Tj+1,…,TkT_{j+1},\ldots,T_{k} lie in HH. Before TjT_{j} was chosen, at most q−2+q=2​q−2q-2+q=2q-2 terms lay outside HH, whereas at least 2​q2−2​q+12q^{2}-2q+1 lay in HH. Distinct subgroups of order qq in G/KG/K meet only at zero, and the remaining terms have nonzero images. Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Choose a basis (x1,…,xr)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}) with ord⁡(xi)=ni\ord(x_{i})=n_{i} and let g0=xrg_{0}=x_{r}, gi=xr+xig_{i}=x_{r}+x_{i} for 1≤i<r1\leq i<r. Thus also a0≡0(modn1)a_{0}\equiv 0\pmod{n_{1}}, and none of the aia_{i} equals nr−1n_{r}-1. This proves 𝖭⁡(G)≥r⁡(nr−1)+1\mathsf{N}(G)\geq r(n_{r}-1)+1. For completeness, consider the direct-sum bound from [4, Theorem 1.1(2)]. A zero-sum subsequence containing all occurrences of some element would therefore have the same property in the corresponding factor, contrary to the choice of the sequences. The product has length ∑i=1r(𝖭⁡(Cni)−1)\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\mathsf{N}(C_{n_{i}})-1), giving the second bound. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

The lower bound for n≥2n\geq 2 follows from Theorem 1.3. For n=1n=1, both stated upper bounds follow from the known value of 𝖭⁡(Cp2)\mathsf{N}(C_{p}^{2}). Fix pp and use strong induction on the integers nn whose prime divisors are at least pp, with the known value of 𝖭⁡(Cp2)\mathsf{N}(C_{p}^{2}) as the base n=1n=1. Thus every multiplicity is strictly smaller than the element order; in particular, 0∤S0\nmid S. If SS is regular, Corollary 4.3 applies.

Otherwise choose HH by Lemma 4.4. Then HH is nontrivial, SHS_{H} is regular over HH, and |SH|≥|H||S_{H}|\geq|H|. First suppose H=Cp⊕Cm​pH=C_{p}\oplus C_{mp} is noncyclic. If m=1m=1, the known value of 𝖭⁡(Cp2)\mathsf{N}(C_{p}^{2}) is at most p2≤|SH|p^{2}\leq|S_{H}|. If m≥2m\geq 2 and p≥5p\geq 5, then |SH|≥m​p2≥ub⁡(H)|S_{H}|\geq mp^{2}\geq\operatorname{ub}(H), so Corollary 4.3, applied within HH, suffices. For p=3p=3, use Lemma 4.8. In each case, 𝗏h​(SH)=𝗏h​(S)\mathsf{v}_{h}(S_{H})=\mathsf{v}_{h}(S) for every h∈Hh\in H, so the subsequence obtained in SHS_{H} also has the required property in SS.

We may therefore suppose H=CmH=C_{m} is cyclic. If |SH|≥𝖭⁡(H)|S_{H}|\geq\mathsf{N}(H), apply its definition within HH. Otherwise m≤|SH|≤𝖭⁡(H)−1m\leq|S_{H}|\leq\mathsf{N}(H)-1. 5. Remarks and open questions

We conjecture that 𝖭⁡(Cp⊕Cn​p)=2​n​p−1\mathsf{N}(C_{p}\oplus C_{np})=2np-1 whenever n≥2n\geq 2 and p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime dividing n​pnp. The non-regular case in the proof of Theorem 1.4 uses only |S|≥2​n​p−1|S|\geq 2np-1. Hence, for the remaining cases p∤np\nmid n, the bound c0​(Cp⊕Cn​p)≤⌈(4​n​p−2)/3⌉c_{0}(C_{p}\oplus C_{np})\leq\lceil(4np-2)/3\rceil would imply the conjecture by Proposition 4.2.

For the cyclic groups below, let An+1=⌈2​n+1⌉A_{n+1}=\lceil 2\sqrt{n+1}\rceil and

Bn+1=min{a+b:a,b∈ℕ,ab≥n+1,gcd(a,n)=1},B_{n+1}=\min\{a+b:a,b\in\mathbb{N},\ ab\geq n+1,\ \gcd(a,n)=1\},

as in [8]. For the following two families, 𝖭⁡(Cn)\mathsf{N}(C_{n}) attains the upper bound 2​n−An+1+12n-A_{n+1}+1 and is strictly larger than 2​n−Bn+1+12n-B_{n+1}+1.

Theorem 5.1.

Let n=2730​(1+105​(2​t−1)​(13​t−13±12))n=2730\bigl(1+105(2t-1)\,(13t-\tfrac{13\pm 1}{2})\bigr) for a positive integer tt; equivalently, n∈T2∪T3n\in T_{2}\cup T_{3}, where

T2\displaystyle T_{2} ={ 2730​(2730​t2−2835​t+736)}t≥1,\displaystyle=\{\,2730(2730t^{2}-2835t+736)\,\}_{t\geq 1},
T3\displaystyle T_{3} ={ 2730​(2730​t2−2625​t+631)}t≥1.\displaystyle=\{\,2730(2730t^{2}-2625t+631)\,\}_{t\geq 1}.

Then

Bn+1=An+1+1=⌈2​n+1⌉+1,B_{n+1}=A_{n+1}+1=\lceil 2\sqrt{n+1}\rceil+1,

and

𝖭⁡(Cn)=2​n−Bn+1+2=2​n−⌈2​n+1⌉+1.\mathsf{N}(C_{n})=2n-B_{n+1}+2=2n-\lceil 2\sqrt{n+1}\rceil+1.
Proof.

By [8, Lemmas 5.2 and 4.3], Bn+1=An+1+1B_{n+1}=A_{n+1}+1 and 𝖭⁡(Cn)≤2​n−An+1+1\mathsf{N}(C_{n})\leq 2n-A_{n+1}+1. Let Cn=⟨e⟩C_{n}=\langle e\rangle.

Suppose first that n∈T2n\in T_{2}, and let d=1365​(2​t−1)−52d=1365(2t-1)-52 and x=(12​n−d)/13x=(12n-d)/13. Then n=d⁡(d−1)−26n=d(d-1)-26, 13|d13\mid d, and dd is odd. Since d≥1313d\geq 1313, we have (d−1)2<n+1<(d−12)2(d-1)^{2}<n+1<(d-\tfrac{1}{2})^{2}, and hence An+1=2​d−1A_{n+1}=2d-1. The identity n=d⁡(d−1)−26n=d(d-1)-26 gives

13​x≡−d(modn),(d−1)​x≡−2(modn).13x\equiv-d\pmod{n},\qquad(d-1)x\equiv-2\pmod{n}.

Every common divisor of xx and nn therefore divides both dd and 22, so gcd⁡(x,n)=1\gcd(x,n)=1. As 1<x<n1<x<n, the sequence S=en−d​(x​e)n−d+1S=e^{n-d}(xe)^{n-d+1} is weak-regular and has length 2​n−An+12n-A_{n+1}. If a zero-sum subsequence contains all n−d+1n-d+1 copies of x​exe, its multiplicity of ee is congruent to (d−1)​x≡−2(modn)(d-1)x\equiv-2\pmod{n}. It must therefore equal n−2>n−dn-2>n-d, a contradiction. If a zero-sum subsequence contains all n−dn-d copies of ee, then 13​x≡−d(modn)13x\equiv-d\pmod{n} and gcd⁡(x,n)=1\gcd(x,n)=1 force its multiplicity of x​exe to equal n−13>n−d+1n-13>n-d+1, also a contradiction.

Suppose now that n∈T3n\in T_{3}, and let d=1365​(2​t−1)+53d=1365(2t-1)+53 and x=(n−d)/2x=(n-d)/2. Then n=d⁡(d−1)−26n=d(d-1)-26, dd is even, and d≡1(mod13)d\equiv 1\pmod{13}. In particular, d≥1418d\geq 1418 and An+1=2​d−1A_{n+1}=2d-1 as above. We have

2​x≡−d(modn),(d−1)​x≡−13(modn).2x\equiv-d\pmod{n},\qquad(d-1)x\equiv-13\pmod{n}.

Every common divisor of xx and nn divides both dd and 1313, so gcd⁡(x,n)=1\gcd(x,n)=1. Again 1<x<n1<x<n, and S=en−d​(x​e)n−d+1S=e^{n-d}(xe)^{n-d+1} is weak-regular with |S|=2​n−An+1|S|=2n-A_{n+1}. A zero-sum subsequence containing all copies of x​exe would have n−13>n−dn-13>n-d copies of ee, by the second congruence. A zero-sum subsequence containing all copies of ee would have n−2>n−d+1n-2>n-d+1 copies of x​exe, by the first congruence and gcd⁡(x,n)=1\gcd(x,n)=1. Thus SS has no zero-sum subsequence TT with 𝗏g​(T)=𝗏g​(S)\mathsf{v}_{g}(T)=\mathsf{v}_{g}(S) for g∈{e,x​e}g\in\{e,xe\}. In both cases, the definition of 𝖭⁡(Cn)\mathsf{N}(C_{n}) gives 𝖭⁡(Cn)≥2​n−An+1+1\mathsf{N}(C_{n})\geq 2n-A_{n+1}+1, proving the equality. ∎

Remark 5.2.

The construction of Theorem 5.1 relies on the specific relation n=d⁡(d−1)−26n=d(d-1)-26 together with the arithmetic of 1313 modulo dd (or d−1d-1). For the other two families T4,T5T_{4},T_{5} identified in [8, Lemma 5.2] (which satisfy n=d2−64n=d^{2}-64 rather than n=d⁡(d−1)−26n=d(d-1)-26), the analogous construction does not apply directly, and whether 𝖭⁡(Cn)\mathsf{N}(C_{n}) on T4∪T5T_{4}\cup T_{5} attains the upper or the lower bound remains an open question.
